title: Looking at Working Memory Another Way
author: Efrat Furst
source: Making Sense of Learning Science (efratfurst.substack.com), March 10, 2026
summary: Efrat Furst proposes rethinking working memory not as a limited container to be protected from overload, but as an active process arising from the interaction between incoming stimuli and activated prior knowledge. She walks through the standard "textbook" multi-store model and Baddeley and Hitch's more detailed multicomponent model before settling on Cowan's Embedded Processes Model, which treats working memory as a function rather than a separate storage compartment: attention activates portions of long-term memory that bind, briefly, with new information. To make this abstract model concrete, Furst extends her "pyramid model" of knowledge construction, illustrating how the same four words can be nearly impossible to retain when they're unfamiliar, weakly remembered when they're familiar but unconnected, and easily bound into memory when they land on a rich, well-rehearsed network of prior knowledge. She uses digit-span demonstrations to show that working memory's real constraint isn't a fixed slot count but how much existing structure incoming information can hook onto. The upshot, Furst argues, is that instructional decisions should focus less on simply "reducing cognitive load" and more on deliberately activating and connecting relevant prior knowledge, since that connection is what determines whether new information gets bound into lasting memory at all.
points: Furst's central reframe is that working memory should be understood as an active binding process between incoming information and activated long-term memory, per Cowan's Embedded Processes Model, rather than as a fixed-capacity container to avoid overloading.

Her three-case digit/word demonstration shows that identical surface conditions (four items to remember) produce wildly different retention depending on how much relevant prior-knowledge structure is already in place to bind them to.

The "reduce cognitive load" heuristic, while simple and actionable, can obscure the more important instructional question of how to activate and connect students' existing knowledge structures to new material.

Furst's pyramid-model illustration reframes chunking as "cementing" -- repeated, connected practice turns a cluster of separate blocks into a single larger unit, which is why experts can hold more inside the same number of working-memory "slots" than novices.
The focus of instruction should shift from managing capacity limitation and cognitive load toward deliberately shaping the interaction between new ideas and prior knowledge.
quotes: Working Memory can be described simply as a limited-capacity mental space where we actively and temporarily manipulate information. Its most recognised features are the limited capacity and the resulting experience of cognitive load. Yet neither is the core feature.
Functional capacity is limited to an average of about seven familiar symbols, such as digits, letters, or words, but only two to four unfamiliar ones. Distractions reduce processing capacity.
In this model, working memory is not a separate store but a function that arises from interactions between incoming stimuli and activated portions of long-term memory within the focus of attention.

New ideas always build on existing ones. A new block "lands" on an existing knowledge base. Creating a pyramid shape represents 'meaning making' - each block can "land" in different places, but when it stacks correctly on relevant prior knowledge and forms a new pyramid, it makes sense!

Because there is little to no relevant prior knowledge, the activated portions of LTM are randomly scattered and unconnected to the new items. The chances for meaningful binding are therefore low, and the activity is unlikely to leave a trace after attention fades.

In this situation, the four words are part of a well-developed expert network. Each word activates not only a single chunk, represented by a larger cemented triangle, but also a broader network of related concepts.

Viewed this way, working memory justifies its name: it's memory at work. It's a function, not a store. The key mechanism is the simultaneous activation of incoming stimuli and existing knowledge structures, which together shape the potential for later memory and performance.
